metadata.title: The Logout That Didn't

metadata.note: AI-EXPLAINER, default fidelity brand, claude-hai channel, Bella. MANDATORY SPINE INTACT: cold open (B00) → body B01-B10 → verdict page (B11) → HANDOFF (B12) → title-restate outro (B13). WAR-STORY SHAPE PRESERVED: the body is deliberately not a feature tour. It runs report (B01/B02) → investigation (B03/B04) → root cause (B05/B06/B07) → fix (B08/B09) → lesson (B10), and each act is allowed to behave like its act: B02 ends on a question rather than an answer, B07 is the reveal, B10 draws the moral. The verdict recaps the INVESTIGATION, not a feature list. ILLUSTRATE LAW: the Claude UI appears only at B00/B11/B12/B13; every body beat is a C3 concept illustration. LOGO LAW: HAI mark as a low-opacity lower-right bug on every beat, full size on B13. OPENING-STATE RULE: every body beat's show block opens with an explicit non-empty t=0 state, and the bookend wrappers carry the haiKit preroll, because the shared Claude scenes otherwise leave blank frames at a cut. VERIFIED FACTS STATED WITHOUT HEDGING (author instruction): signOut({redirectUrl}) is live on main raced against a 5s timeout with a fallback redirect, merged via PR #14 on 2026-10-13; the old no-Clerk-signOut comment is gone from main. OPEN ITEM, NOT A RESOLVED FACT: PR #13 (same fix, targeting development) was re-checked live at build time — state OPEN, mergedAt null, mergeStateStatus CLEAN — and development's LogoutButton.tsx still has no signOut call and still carries the stale comment. The caveat is therefore carried on screen at B09 and spoken at both B09 and B11. If #13 merges before publish, re-record B09 and B11 and re-render those two beats only. NO OVERCLAIM: B11 states explicitly that textbook token revocation always worked (the subject of the One Sign-In, Many Books reel) and that it was the hub's own session that survived logout, so neither video contradicts the other and nothing here says logout is fully solved. NAMING: narration says 'the identity provider' rather than naming the vendor, following the author's script.

beats.narration_text: Hi — this is Bella, for Chaitanya. A bug report: the Logout button logs nobody out. Every user, every time, and only in production. This is the postmortem — what broke, and why it was invisible where you'd look.

the ask types itself in, character by character
send arms terracotta; runningText 'reading the postmortem…'
three result lines land in order — the ask comes back ANSWERED, so the reel opens on a finding, not a question
HAI bug settles lower-right

props.command: Our Logout button redirects but leaves every user signed in — in production only. It works on my laptop and the logout code hasn't changed in months. Walk me through how I would actually find this.
output: the button deleted the evidence — it never ended the session
moving to the production instance moved where the session lives

beats.narration_text: Someone clicks Logout. The page redirects. And they're still signed in. Not a rare edge case, not a flaky one — every time, for everyone, on the live site. The button does something; it just doesn't do what it says.

show.event: OPENING STATE IS NOT EMPTY: a browser card is already drawn, signed-in chip lit in the corner, Logout button in place
the button depresses
the page wipes and reloads
the signed-in chip is STILL LIT after the reload — the failure is watched, not described
a counter of repeated attempts ticks up, every one ending signed in

beats.narration_text: And here's what makes it interesting. The same code, on a developer's laptop, logged out perfectly. It had worked for months, and nothing in the logout code had changed. So before you read a line of it: whatever's wrong here probably isn't the code.

show.event: OPENING STATE IS NOT EMPTY: two panes already framed and headed — LAPTOP and LIVE SITE — each showing the identical logout code block, unread
the laptop pane resolves to a green signed-out state
a months-long unchanged timeline draws beneath both panes
the two code blocks are marked IDENTICAL — same bytes, different outcome
the code blocks grey out and the two ENVIRONMENT labels take the accent instead — the investigation turns

props.turnNote: so look at the environment, not the code

beats.narration_text: On paper the button did a thorough job. It called the server to record that you'd logged out. Then it walked every cookie it could see and deleted it — plain domain, parent domain, localhost. Cleared local storage, cleared session storage, and redirected you home.

show.event: OPENING STATE IS NOT EMPTY: the full cleanup checklist is already drawn, every row present and unticked
row one ticks
row two ticks
row three ticks
row four ticks
row five ticks
row six ticks
the list reports complete, every row green — the beat deliberately looks like a success

props.title: what logout did
rows: tell the server I logged out

beats.narration_text: What it never did was ask the identity provider to actually end the session. It cleaned up every piece of evidence that you were logged in, by hand, and assumed that was the same thing. For months, it was.

show.event: OPENING STATE IS NOT EMPTY: the completed green checklist from B03 is still on screen, carried over so the reveal has something to land against
a seventh row slides in beneath the six — unticked, terracotta: 'ask the provider to end the session'
the six ticked rows are re-labelled as a group: EVIDENCE
an equals sign between EVIDENCE and SESSION is struck through
the struck equals briefly flickers back — it really had been equivalent, until it wasn't

beats.narration_text: Then the project moved from the provider's development setup to its production one. Different infrastructure — and a different place to keep the session. Nobody touched the logout code. The ground moved under it.

show.event: OPENING STATE IS NOT EMPTY: the app sits on a labelled platform marked DEVELOPMENT SETUP, with the logout code pinned to it
the platform slides out and a PRODUCTION SETUP platform slides in beneath the same app

show.at: on 'a different place to keep the session'

the pinned code block is stamped UNCHANGED — it never moves in the whole beat
the platform settles in terracotta; the code stays exactly where it was

beats.narration_text: On the development setup the session cookie lived on the app's own domain. Page JavaScript could see it, so deleting it by hand worked. On production the session lives on a different domain — the provider's own — and it's marked HttpOnly. Page JavaScript cannot read it or delete it. That's not a bug; that's the point of the flag. It's what stops a malicious script stealing your session.

show.event: OPENING STATE IS NOT EMPTY: both diagrams are already framed and headed — DEVELOPMENT left, PRODUCTION right — each with its app box and a cookie slot drawn
the left cookie lands inside the app's own boundary
a reach from page JavaScript touches it; it clears
the right cookie lands OUTSIDE the app boundary, on the provider's
an HttpOnly tag clips onto the right cookie in terracotta

show.at: on 'cannot read it or delete it'

the blocked reach is RE-LABELLED from a failure to a defence — same picture, opposite reading

props.defenceNote: this is what stops a malicious script stealing your session

beats.narration_text: So the loop ran, deleted everything it could reach, reported success — and the one cookie that mattered sat there untouched. Reload, and the provider helpfully signs you back in. The code wasn't wrong. Its assumption about where the session lived was.

show.event: OPENING STATE IS NOT EMPTY: a row of cookies sits drawn inside the reachable boundary, with one more outside it, all present
the inside cookies grey out one by one
a green SUCCESS stamp lands — on a job that did not do the thing
the outside cookie is ringed terracotta, untouched, while everything else is dead
a reload arc runs and the signed-in chip relights from that one surviving cookie

show.at: on 'assumption about where the session lived'
show.event: the word ASSUMPTION replaces the word CODE under the diagnosis line

beats.narration_text: The fix is one line in spirit: actually call the provider's sign-out. But look at how it's written. The call is raced against a five-second timer, and if it loses, the code redirects you anyway. Signing out is a network call to someone else's service — if that service is slow, you don't want a user stranded on a page that won't let them leave.

show.event: OPENING STATE IS NOT EMPTY: two lanes already drawn and labelled — SIGN OUT and 5-SECOND TIMER — both at the start line, with one finish marked REDIRECT
the sign-out lane begins advancing
the timer lane advances alongside it, a real race
the timer lane reaches the line first in this run; the sign-out lane is cut short
BOTH lanes converge on the same REDIRECT outcome — the point is that either path ends with the user out
a stranded-user state is shown greyed and crossed — the outcome the race exists to prevent

beats.narration_text: The cookie loop stayed, by the way — it isn't what fixes this, but it's harmless and it covers the local case. And one thing is still live as I record. The fix is on main. The development branch does not have it yet, so the next release cut from development would bring the bug straight back.

beats.narration_text: Two things to take away. Don't reimplement what a library already does, especially security. The manual cleanup looked more thorough than one function call; it wasn't, it was more code doing less. And this bug could not be found in development — the environments differed in exactly the way the broken assumption depended on. That's the dangerous kind.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. The button deleted every trace of the session it could reach, and never asked the provider to end it. That worked until the session moved to a domain the page can't touch. And be precise about what's fixed: logging out always revoked textbook access correctly. It was the hub's own session that survived, and that half is fixed on main — development is still waiting.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Take this into Claude: My logout clears cookies and local storage by hand instead of calling my auth provider's sign-out. Tell me what that breaks once the session cookie is HttpOnly and on the provider's own domain, and what else in my app might be assuming state lives somewhere it no longer does. That last clause is the one to push on. This was never really a bug about logout.
